summaries.gardner: Micron shows several Rule Breaker traits today: very strong price momentum (shares up about 425% over the 52 weeks to October 2026) and a central role in the AI build-out through HBM. But it is a 40-plus-year-old memory maker in a cyclical, commodity-like industry rather than the top dog and first mover in an emerging one, and analysts mostly call it cheap rather than overvalued.
summaries.buffett: Micron fits Buffett's approach poorly despite record FY2026 results ($133.2B revenue, $85.0B net income): memory prices are set by industry supply, and the company lost $5.8B as recently as FY2023. Buffett avoids businesses whose earnings swing this widely and require constant heavy capital spending ($27.4B of net capex in FY2026).
summaries.munger: Munger would credit Micron's place in a three-player DRAM oligopoly and its strong balance sheet, but he was wary of capital-intensive commodity businesses where gains get competed away. Inverting the problem, a return to oversupply as Samsung, SK hynix, CXMT and Micron itself add capacity is a clear way for today's profits to shrink sharply.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify Micron as a cyclical, and he warned that cyclicals look cheapest on P/E (about 12.8 trailing and 5.4 forward in October 2026) near the top of the cycle. The PEG ratio of about 0.08 looks extremely attractive, but his rule for cyclicals is to judge where the cycle stands, and memory revenue has already more than tripled in one year.
summaries.fisher: Micron scores well on Fisher's points about R&D results and new products: it was first to ship 1-beta and 1-gamma DRAM and built an HBM business qualified at NVIDIA. It scores weaker on steady profit margins and long-term growth, because results swing sharply with memory prices, as the FY2023 operating margin of about -37% showed.
summaries.graham: Micron fails most of Graham's defensive tests: it lost money in FY2016 and FY2023, has paid dividends only since 2021, and trades at about 35 times average FY2024-FY2026 earnings with P/E times P/B near 100. It passes on size and on EPS growth, which went from a loss of $0.27 in FY2016 to $74.33 in FY2026.
summaries.thiel: Micron does not fit Thiel's monopoly ideal: it is the number three in DRAM (22.4% share in 4Q25) and HBM (about 21%), with no technology ten times better than Samsung's or SK hynix's. It does score well on timing, durability of the oligopoly and the importance of the problem it solves for AI computing.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner's focus on platform shifts, especially AI, favours Micron as a key supplier of HBM and data-center memory, and its free-cash-flow yield of about 5.5% looks reasonable on current results. The risk is that FY2026 marks a cyclical peak in memory prices, so today's cash flow may not be durable.
summaries.druckenmiller: Micron fits Druckenmiller's style unusually well right now: earnings are accelerating (Q1 FY2027 revenue guidance of $61.5B vs $54.2B in Q4 FY2026), estimates have risen and the stock has strong momentum. He would also watch closely for signs of the next memory downturn, since cyclical stocks often peak before earnings do.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids cyclical, capital-intensive businesses; even though Micron's FY2026 gross margin (80.7%) and ROIC (about 93%) are extraordinary, they follow a year with a negative gross margin in FY2023. Its returns are not consistent enough over a cycle to fit Fundsmith's criteria.
summaries.greenblatt: On trailing figures Micron would rank near the top of a Magic Formula screen, with ROIC of about 93% and EV/EBIT of about 10. Greenblatt cautions that peak-cycle earnings can mislead, but the formula itself would currently favour it.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool needs a great business, honest management and strong reinvestment; Micron has capable management and large reinvestment opportunities in new US fabs, but the business leg is weak because returns swing with the memory cycle. Insider ownership is only about 0.2%.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach favours simple businesses bought cheaply in distress; Micron was such a candidate in the FY2023 downturn, but after a roughly 425% one-year rise it is priced near peak earnings. The low forward P/E carries the risk of a sharp fall if memory prices drop.
summaries.wood: Micron fits Cathie Wood's AI theme as a supplier of HBM and server memory that AI accelerators need, and memory costs per bit fall with each node. It is an enabler of AI rather than a platform innovator, and ARK's framework values companies that combine several innovation platforms, which Micron does not.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with moats; Micron's cash flow is large today ($59.0B of FCF in FY2026) but highly unpredictable over the cycle. Its strong balance sheet ($43.4B of cash and short-term investments vs $5.2B of debt) is a plus, but predictability is not.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep looked for scale economies shared with customers in ever-strengthening businesses; memory makers pass cost savings to customers only when competition forces them to, and pricing power depends on industry supply. Micron's position is not clearly getting stronger relative to SK hynix and Samsung.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed companies attacking large, painful problems in huge markets, and AI's demand for memory bandwidth is such a problem, with memory chip sales forecast near $800B for 2026. But Micron is a mature, cyclical manufacturer rather than an early-stage company with breakthrough products.
summaries.nash: Micron passes most of Tom Nash's current-numbers tests: FY2026 revenue grew 256% to $133.2B with a 74.6% operating margin, it now holds $43.4B of cash against $5.2B of debt and it has beaten EPS estimates for five straight quarters. Its weak points are its cyclical memory business: revenue fell 49% in FY2023, cash was below debt until early 2026 and CEO Sanjay Mehrotra is a hired manager who sells shares. The PEG of 0.08 and reverse DCF look cheap, but a bear-case DCF on its 3-year average FCF margin gives about $596 a share, below the $953.19 price.

momentum.evidence: MU rose about 425% over the 52 weeks to October 13, 2026 (to $953.19), versus about a 20.4% total return for the S&P 500 (SPY).

g4.evidence: CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, a SanDisk co-founder, has led a strong turnaround since 2017, and NVIDIA is a key HBM partner, but Micron is not backed by famous lead investors.

g6.evidence: Most analysts call the stock cheap, citing a forward P/E of about 5.4, though some warn that memory earnings may be near a cyclical peak.

simple.evidence: Micron's products (DRAM, HBM, NAND) are easy to describe, but forecasting memory prices and the industry cycle is hard even for specialists.

b2.evidence: Revenue fell 49% in FY2023 to $15.5B with a $5.8B net loss, before soaring to $133.2B in FY2026.

integrity.evidence: Management is credible and reports clearly, but insiders own only about 0.2% and the CEO has sold shares under a trading plan in 2026.

b6.evidence: Micron stays focused on memory and storage rather than diversifying into unrelated businesses.

roic.evidence: Trailing ROIC is about 93% with little debt ($5.2B), but returns were negative in FY2023, so they are not consistent.

fcf.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was $59.0B, about 69% of its $85.0B net income, despite $27.4B of net capex.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings funded the node and HBM investments behind FY2026's record results, and its market value of about $1.1 trillion is far above the earnings it has retained.

safety.evidence: The forward P/E of about 5.4 looks cheap, but at about 7.8 times book value and peak-cycle earnings the price is not clearly below a conservative through-cycle value.

fairprice.evidence: About 12.8 times trailing earnings is low for its current growth, but a through-cycle net margin closer to 30% (vs 64% in FY2026) would make it much less cheap.

mu5.evidence: Oversupply from new fabs, SK hynix's HBM lead, state-backed Chinese rivals (CXMT, YMTC), an AI spending slowdown and geopolitics are all real failure paths for its profits.

reinvest.evidence: Micron is investing heavily in new fabs in Idaho and New York, but returns on that capital depend on future memory prices.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic cyclical: revenue fell 49% in FY2023 and then rose from $25.1B in FY2024 to $133.2B in FY2026 as memory prices recovered.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 12.8 is far below EPS growth (from $7.59 in FY2025 to $74.33 in FY2026), with a PEG of about 0.08, though Lynch warned low P/Es on cyclicals can mark a peak.

runway.evidence: AI demand could keep memory growing (consensus FY2027 revenue about $275B), but revenue will likely fall again in the next downturn.

ly7.evidence: CEO Sanjay Mehrotra sold shares under a trading plan in 2026, and the share count rose about 1.6% over the past year.

ly8.evidence: Micron is followed by about 40 analysts and is a widely discussed AI stock.

fi2.evidence: Micron moved from HBM3E to HBM4 and custom HBM4E base dies, and keeps launching new DRAM and NAND nodes as older products mature.

fi3.evidence: Its R&D made it first to ship 1-beta and 1-gamma DRAM and won HBM qualification on NVIDIA platforms.

fi4.evidence: Micron sells HBM under annual contracts and is sold out, but customers deliberately spread purchases across Samsung, SK hynix and Micron.

longterm.evidence: Mehrotra has committed about $200B to US manufacturing and R&D over many years, accepting heavy capex for long-term position.

gr1.evidence: Micron had $133.2B of revenue in FY2026 and about 61,000 employees.

ni10.evidence: Micron lost $276M in FY2016 and $5.8B in FY2023.

gr4.evidence: Micron only began paying a quarterly dividend in 2021.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS went from a loss of $0.27 in FY2016 to $74.33 in FY2026.

gr6.evidence: Average EPS for FY2024-FY2026 ($0.70, $7.59, $74.33) is about $27.54, so the $953.19 price is about 35 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 12.8 times a P/B of about 7.8 gives roughly 100, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Micron's DRAM and HBM are competitive with Samsung's and SK hynix's, but not ten times better; SK hynix leads HBM with about 57% share.

timing.evidence: AI accelerators need ever more HBM and server memory, and memory chip sales are forecast near $800B for 2026 versus $230B in 2025.

th3.evidence: Micron competes in a large, established memory market where it ranks third, rather than dominating a small market.

team.evidence: Sanjay Mehrotra, a SanDisk co-founder and engineer, has run Micron well since 2017, but the team is not seen as exceptional founder-led leadership.

th5.evidence: Micron sells directly to hyperscalers, NVIDIA and device makers under qualification and annual contracts, and has the Crucial consumer brand.

durable.evidence: The three-player DRAM oligopoly has lasted for over a decade, but Chinese entrants such as CXMT and the cycle make its long-term position less certain.

th7.evidence: The AI memory opportunity is widely recognised and pursued by Samsung and SK hynix as well.

trend.evidence: Micron is one of only three suppliers of HBM for AI accelerators, and cloud and AI data-center memory made up about 32% of revenue in FY2026.

dr1.evidence: EPS rose from $7.59 in FY2025 to $74.33 in FY2026, Q1 FY2027 revenue guidance is $61.5B vs $54.2B in Q4 FY2026, and FY2027 estimates have risen.

dr2.evidence: Contracted HBM demand and higher guidance support further gains, but new industry capacity could turn the memory cycle within 18-24 months.

dr4.evidence: Strong AI capex by hyperscalers supports demand, but memory demand from PCs, phones and industry is sensitive to the economy.

dr6.evidence: HBM4 ramps on new NVIDIA platforms, annual HBM contract pricing and quarterly guidance are identifiable drivers.

dr7.evidence: Momentum and earnings revisions are strong, but the cyclical risk argues against a very large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 80.7% in FY2026, but it was negative in FY2023, so it reflects the price cycle more than lasting pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of $59.0B gives an FCF yield of about 5.5%.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 10.2, an operating earnings yield of about 10% on enterprise value, though on peak-cycle earnings.

pa2.evidence: Micron is at record results rather than in a temporary setback; the FY2023 downturn has already been reversed.

pa4.evidence: Its strong balance sheet limits business risk, but buying near peak earnings risks large share-price losses if memory prices fall.

wo1.evidence: Micron is a leading supplier of memory for AI, but it is an enabler of AI rather than a leader in AI platforms themselves.

wo2.evidence: Cost per bit falls with each new DRAM and NAND node, but current demand growth is driven by AI rather than falling memory costs.

wo3.evidence: Micron focuses on one platform, memory and storage.

wo4.evidence: The AI memory market has grown very fast (forecast near $800B in 2026), but it is not likely to be many times larger again in five years.

ac3.evidence: Memory is commodity-like, so Micron's revenue and margins swing with industry prices, as the FY2023 negative gross margin showed.

ns1.evidence: Micron prices at what the market bears, raising prices sharply in shortages rather than sharing scale savings with customers.

ns4.evidence: New US fabs and HBM4 could strengthen it, but SK hynix leads HBM and Chinese makers are adding capacity.

va2.evidence: AI computing is limited by memory bandwidth and capacity, and HBM directly addresses that bottleneck for NVIDIA and other accelerator makers.

tn1.evidence: Micron is one of three suppliers of HBM memory for AI accelerators, part of the AI infrastructure layer, but it is a memory maker founded in 1978 that adapted to AI rather than a company built for it.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew from $15,540M in FY2023 to $133,188M in FY2026, net income was $84,969M in FY2026 and cash ($43,434M) exceeds debt ($5,179M).

tn11.evidence: Micron provides DRAM, HBM and NAND memory that help AI data centres, PC and phone makers store and move data quickly, and it charges per chip, increasingly under long-term supply agreements.

tn18.evidence: Sanjay Mehrotra has delivered strong growth and an HBM turnaround since 2017, but he has been CEO for about 9 years, did not found Micron (he co-founded SanDisk) and sells shares under a trading plan.
